# Named Effects in Behavioral Science {#effects}

A software company adds a "Pro" plan that almost no one buys, and sales of its
"Business" plan rise. A furniture retailer sells flat-packed products that
customers must assemble themselves, and customers seem to like them more for the
trouble. A soft-drink brand that has advertised the same slogan for years worries
that its campaign has "worn out", while a challenger worries that no one has heard
of it at all. A board appoints its first female chief executive just as the firm
enters a crisis. Behavioural scientists have a name for each of these patterns,
the **decoy effect**, the **IKEA effect**, **mere exposure** and **wear-out**, the
**glass cliff**, and much of applied behavioural science consists of recognising
such patterns and knowing when they will and will not appear.

This chapter is a field guide to named effects that recur in management,
marketing, and organisational research. A named effect is not the same thing as a
theory. An effect is a **reliable empirical regularity**: a pattern linking a
manipulation or condition to an outcome. A theory explains *why* the regularity
occurs and therefore predicts *when* it will occur. Many effects in this chapter
have several candidate explanations, and part of the craft of using them is
connecting each effect to the mechanisms developed elsewhere in the book:
[processing fluency](#processing-fluency), [prospect theory](#prospect-theory),
[signaling](#signaling-theory), and [social identity](#social-identity-theory).
Social facilitation, a close relative of several effects here, is covered with
social influence in [Social facilitation](#social-facilitation).

```{r tab-eff-catalogue}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Effect, ~`One-line definition`, ~`Key source`, ~`Business use`, ~`Evidence strength`,
  "Mere exposure", "Repeated exposure to a stimulus increases liking for it", "Zajonc (1968), Bornstein (1989)", "Ad frequency, brand familiarity", "Strong (meta-analytic)",
  "Warm-glow heuristic", "Positive stimuli feel more familiar, even without prior exposure", "Monin (2003)", "Brand familiarity judgments, recognition research", "Moderate (focused programme)",
  "Goldilocks (inverted-U)", "Liking peaks at moderate novelty or complexity", "Berlyne (1970), McCall & McGhee (1977)", "Product and ad design, innovation newness", "Moderate, shape depends on measure",
  "Coolidge", "Renewed sexual interest with a novel partner (non-human animals)", "Wilson, Kuehn & Beach (1963), Dewsbury (1981)", "Analogy for variety seeking and novelty in product lines", "Strong in animals, analogical for consumers",
  "Bandwagon / snob / Veblen", "Demand rises or falls with others' consumption or with price itself", "Leibenstein (1950)", "Luxury pricing, scarcity, network goods", "Strong theoretical basis, mixed measurement",
  "Glass cliff", "Women and minorities are disproportionately appointed to precarious leadership roles", "Ryan & Haslam (2005)", "Succession and board decisions", "Moderate, context-dependent",
  "IKEA effect", "Labour invested in creating a product increases its valuation", "Norton, Mochon & Ariely (2012)", "Self-assembly, co-creation, customisation", "Moderate",
  "Decoy (attraction)", "Adding a dominated option increases choice of the option that dominates it", "Huber, Payne & Puto (1982)", "Pricing tiers and product line design", "Contested, strongest with numeric attributes",
  "Anchoring", "Estimates are biased toward an initially considered number", "Tversky & Kahneman (1974)", "Reference prices, negotiation, forecasting", "Strong (multi-lab replication)",
  "Beauty in averageness", "Averaged or prototypical stimuli are judged attractive", "Langlois & Roggman (1990)", "Product design typicality", "Strong for faces, moderate for products",

The evidence-strength column is a summary judgment, not a formal rating. It
reflects the size and consistency of the literature, the existence of
meta-analyses or multi-laboratory replications, and known disputes about
robustness. Section \@ref(effects-replication) returns to the question of how
much confidence to place in named effects.

## Mere Exposure Effect {#mere-exposure-effect}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Repeated exposure to a stimulus, without any reinforcement,
increases liking for it.

**Origins.** Social psychology, @zajonc1968, meta-analysed by @bornstein1989 and,
with a focus on the shape of the exposure-liking curve, by @montoya2017.

**Level of analysis.** Individual perceiver.

**Key constructs.** Exposure frequency, stimulus complexity, exposure duration,
recognition, familiarity, liking, boredom (tedium).

**Boundary conditions.** Strongest for initially neutral or unfamiliar stimuli,
brief exposures, and complex stimuli. Weak or reversed for initially disliked
stimuli and after many exposures, when tedium sets in.

**Related theories.** [Processing fluency](#processing-fluency),
[Warm-glow heuristic](#warm-glow-heuristic), [Goldilocks effect](#goldilocks-effect),
[Elaboration likelihood model](#elaboration-likelihood-model).
:::

### Core logic and evidence

@zajonc1968 proposed that "mere repeated exposure" of an individual to a stimulus
is a sufficient condition for enhancing his or her attitude toward it. He combined
correlational evidence, words that appear more frequently in natural language
tend to have more positive meanings, with experiments in which participants saw
nonsense words, Chinese-like characters, or photographs of faces between zero and
25 times and then rated how much they liked them or how "good" their meaning was.
Ratings rose with frequency of exposure. The finding was striking because it
required no reward, no persuasive argument, and no conscious evaluation: frequency
alone was enough.

Later work showed that the effect does not require conscious recognition.
@kunstwilson1980 presented irregular polygons so briefly that participants could
not recognise them above chance later. Nonetheless, when asked which of two
polygons they *liked* more, participants tended to prefer the ones they had seen
before. @bornstein1989 reviewed the first two decades of research and concluded
that the effect is robust across stimuli and settings. His meta-analysis also
identified moderators that remain central to applied work: the effect is stronger
for brief exposures and for stimuli that are not consciously recognised, stronger
for complex than for simple stimuli, and tends to level off after a moderate
number of exposures, with very long exposure sequences producing smaller effects.

### Mechanism

Two broad explanations dominate. The **fluency** account holds that prior exposure
makes a stimulus easier to perceive and process, and that this ease is experienced
as a mildly positive feeling that is attributed to the stimulus itself
[@reber2004]. The account explains why the effect is stronger when people do not
recognise the stimulus: if people realise that a stimulus feels easy *because* they
have seen it before, they discount the feeling. The **two-factor** account adds a
second process. Exposure produces positive habituation (reduced uncertainty and
increasing fluency) but also **tedium**: boredom that accumulates with repetition.
Liking is the net of the two, so it first rises and then falls. @cacioppo1979
documented the pattern for persuasive messages: agreement with a message rose from
one to three presentations and then fell at five, while counter-arguments followed
the opposite pattern. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-eff-exposure) illustrates the
two-factor logic.

```{r fig-eff-exposure, fig.cap = "Stylised two-factor model of repetition. Positive habituation rises quickly and saturates, tedium accumulates with repetition. Net liking first rises (wear-in) and then declines (wear-out). Curves are illustrative functions, not estimates.", fig.height = 4}
n <- seq(0, 20, by = 0.1)
habituation <- 10 * (1 - exp(-n / 3))
tedium <- 0.03 * n^2
expo <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(n, value = habituation, component = "Positive habituation (fluency)"),
  data.frame(n, value = tedium, component = "Tedium (boredom)"),
  data.frame(n, value = habituation - tedium, component = "Net liking")
) |>
  mutate(component = factor(component, levels = c("Net liking", "Positive habituation (fluency)", "Tedium (boredom)")))
peak <- n[which.max(habituation - tedium)]
ggplot(expo, aes(n, value, colour = component, linetype = component)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = peak, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = pal[["blue"]], alpha = 0.05) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = peak, colour = ink[["muted"]], linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = peak / 2, y = 11.5, label = "Wear-in", size = 3.4, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = peak + (20 - peak) / 2, y = 11.5, label = "Wear-out", size = 3.4, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(pal[["blue"]], pal[["orange"]], pal[["aqua"]])) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed", "dashed")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-3, 12.5)) +
  labs(x = "Number of exposures", y = "Affective response (arbitrary units)", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL,
       title = "Repetition helps, then hurts",
       caption = "Stylised: habituation = 10(1 - exp(-n/3)), tedium = 0.03n^2.")
```

Table \@ref(tab:tab-eff-exposure) summarises the moderators most relevant to
practice.

```{r tab-eff-exposure}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Moderator, ~`Direction of effect`, ~`Likely mechanism`, ~`Managerial implication`,
  "Number of exposures", "Rises, then levels off or declines", "Habituation versus tedium", "Plan frequency caps, monitor wear-out",
  "Stimulus complexity", "Larger effect for complex stimuli", "Complex stimuli take longer to become boring", "Richer creative executions sustain repetition",
  "Exposure duration / awareness", "Larger for brief, unrecognised exposures", "Fluency is misattributed when its source is not noticed", "Background placements can build familiarity",
  "Initial valence", "Weak or reversed for initially disliked stimuli", "Repetition can intensify an existing reaction", "Do not repeat a disliked execution",
  "Variation across exposures", "Varied executions delay wear-out", "Reduces tedium while preserving the core stimulus", "Rotate creative around a constant brand cue"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Moderators of the mere exposure effect (synthesised from Bornstein, 1989, and the two-factor literature).")
```

::: {.business-case}
**Brand familiarity and ad repetition: wear-in and wear-out.** Media planners
work with the two-factor curve every day, even when they do not call it that. A new
brand needs **wear-in**: enough exposures for consumers to recognise the brand and
to process its logo and packaging fluently. An established campaign risks
**wear-out**: after many exposures, the same execution bores or irritates, and
consumers begin to counter-argue. Practitioners respond in three ways that follow
directly from the moderators above. They set **frequency caps** in digital
campaigns to limit how often one person sees an advertisement. They **rotate
creative executions** that vary the surface while holding constant the brand cues
that should become familiar, and they invest in **distinctive brand assets**,
colours, shapes, sonic logos, that accumulate familiarity across many different
executions. The mere exposure effect also cautions against a naive reading of
brand-tracking data: familiarity can raise liking without any change in beliefs
about the product, so rising preference is not necessarily evidence that the
message was understood.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Liking for a new package design will increase over the first several
  exposures and decline thereafter, with the peak occurring later for more complex
  designs.
- *H2.* Varying advertising executions while holding the brand cue constant will
  delay wear-out relative to repeating a single execution.

**Designs.** Repeated-exposure experiments with incidental exposure tasks. Field
data linking advertising frequency to brand metrics with exposure-level variation.
Response-latency measures of fluency.

**Measures.** Liking ratings, implicit preference measures, recognition, processing
speed, brand-tracking familiarity and favourability.
:::

## Warm-Glow Heuristic {#warm-glow-heuristic}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** The positive valence of a stimulus increases its perceived
familiarity, even when the person has never encountered it before. Familiarity
breeds liking, but liking also breeds a feeling of familiarity.

**Origins.** Social cognition, @Monin_2003.

**Level of analysis.** Individual perceiver.

**Key constructs.** Stimulus valence (attractiveness, positivity), perceived
familiarity, recognition judgments, misattribution of affect.

**Boundary conditions.** Most pronounced when people have little diagnostic memory
information and must rely on feelings to judge whether something is familiar.

**Related theories.** [Mere exposure](#mere-exposure-effect),
[Discrepancy attribution hypothesis](#discrepancy-attribution-hypothesis),
[Feelings-as-information theory](#feelings-as-information-theory),
[Processing fluency](#processing-fluency).
:::

### Core logic and evidence

The mere exposure effect runs from familiarity to liking. @Monin_2003 asked whether
the arrow can also run in the opposite direction. In a series of studies he found
that attractive faces were judged more familiar than less attractive faces, and
positive words were more likely than neutral or negative words to be mistakenly
"recognised" as having appeared earlier, even when none of the stimuli had been
shown before. He called this the **warm-glow heuristic**: people experience a
positive affective glow and use it, among other cues, to infer that a stimulus is
familiar. The account is a form of **misattribution**: a feeling that arises from
one source (the stimulus's positivity) is attributed to another (past exposure).

The warm-glow heuristic completes a loop. Familiar things feel easy to process and
are liked. Liked things feel familiar. Each process can reinforce the other, which
helps explain why well-liked brands are often over-estimated in familiarity and why
it is difficult to disentangle familiarity from liking in survey measures.

::: {.pitfall}
**Confusing the warm-glow heuristic with warm-glow giving.** The phrase "warm glow"
is used for two unrelated ideas. @Monin_2003's **warm-glow heuristic** is a
cognitive effect in which positive stimuli feel familiar. @andreoni1990's
**warm-glow giving** is an economic model of charitable behaviour in which donors
derive utility from the act of giving itself, not only from the total amount of
the public good provided: a form of **impure altruism**. Andreoni's model explains,
for example, why government contributions to a public good do not fully crowd out
private donations. Citing one when the argument requires the other is a common
error in student and practitioner writing. Table \@ref(tab:tab-eff-warmglow)
distinguishes them.
:::

```{r tab-eff-warmglow}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Feature, ~`Warm-glow heuristic`, ~`Warm-glow giving`,
  "Discipline", "Social cognition / psychology", "Public economics",
  "Key source", "Monin (2003)", "Andreoni (1990)",
  "Phenomenon", "Positive stimuli are judged more familiar", "People enjoy the act of giving itself",
  "Mechanism", "Misattribution of positive affect to familiarity", "Utility from one's own contribution (impure altruism)",
  "Typical outcome", "Familiarity and recognition judgments", "Donations, crowding-out of private giving",
  "Business application", "Interpreting brand-familiarity and recognition data", "Designing donation appeals and cause marketing"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Two different \"warm glows\".")
```

::: {.business-case}
**Measuring brand awareness.** Brand-tracking surveys often ask respondents
whether they have heard of a brand (aided awareness) and how they feel about it.
The warm-glow heuristic implies that the two answers are not independent:
respondents who like a brand's name, logo, or category may report familiarity with
it even without prior exposure. One practical safeguard is to include **foil
brands**, plausible but fictitious names, in awareness questions. The rate of
"recognition" of foils estimates the false-alarm rate, and positive-sounding foils
are likely to attract more false recognition than neutral ones. Comparing real
brands against valence-matched foils yields a cleaner awareness estimate.
:::

## Goldilocks Effect {#goldilocks-effect}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Many affective and attentional responses follow an **inverted-U**:
people prefer stimuli that are moderately novel, complex, or discrepant from what
they know, not too familiar, not too strange, but "just right".

**Origins.** Experimental aesthetics [@berlyne1970; @berlyne1971], developmental
psychology [@McCall_1977; @kidd2012], the "just right" label was popularised in
consumer behaviour by @Berger_2016.

**Level of analysis.** Individual perceiver.

**Key constructs.** Novelty, complexity, arousal potential, schema discrepancy,
familiarity, optimal level of stimulation.

**Boundary conditions.** The location of the peak depends on the perceiver's
expertise and prior exposure. Some measures (such as typicality-based preference)
show monotonic rather than inverted-U patterns.

**Related theories.** [Mere exposure](#mere-exposure-effect),
[Beauty in averageness](#beauty-in-averageness),
[Optimal distinctiveness theory](#optimal-distinctiveness-theory),
[Hedonic adaptation](#hedonic-adaptation).
:::

### Origins and core logic

The idea that hedonic value peaks at intermediate stimulation is old, it is often
represented as the **Wundt curve**, but its modern form owes most to Daniel
Berlyne's psychobiological aesthetics. @berlyne1971 argued that stimulus properties
such as novelty, complexity, surprisingness, and ambiguity jointly determine a
stimulus's **arousal potential**, and that hedonic value is highest at moderate
arousal potential. @berlyne1970 examined how novelty and complexity interact with
exposure: repeated exposure tended to make simpler patterns less pleasing while
more complex patterns retained or gained appeal, because complex patterns take
longer to become fully familiar.

Developmental psychologists reached a similar conclusion about attention. The
**discrepancy hypothesis** holds that infants attend most to stimuli that are
moderately discrepant from their existing schemas. Stimuli that match a schema
exactly are uninteresting, and stimuli that are wildly discrepant cannot be
assimilated [@McCall_1977]. @kidd2012 provided a modern test using an
information-theoretic measure of how predictable each event in a visual sequence
was. Infants were least likely to look away from sequences of intermediate
predictability, and more likely to look away when events were either highly
predictable or highly surprising: a "Goldilocks effect" in attention.

In consumer research, @meyerslevy1989 found an analogous pattern for product
evaluation: products that were **moderately incongruent** with their category
schema were evaluated more favourably than products that were fully congruent or
extremely incongruent, because moderate incongruity can be resolved and the
resolution is itself rewarding. @Berger_2016 summarises the general lesson for
social influence: things that are too novel feel unfamiliar and uneasy. Things
that are too familiar feel boring. Optimal appeal lies in between.

```{r fig-eff-goldilocks, fig.cap = "Illustrative inverted-U between novelty and liking. With repeated exposure, simple stimuli become boring and the preferred level of novelty shifts upward. Curves are stylised functions, points are simulated ratings.", fig.height = 4}
set.seed(1970)
novelty <- seq(0, 10, by = 0.05)
curve_df <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(novelty, liking = 6 * exp(-(novelty - 3.8)^2 / (2 * 1.9^2)) + 1, stage = "First encounter"),
  data.frame(novelty, liking = 6 * exp(-(novelty - 6.0)^2 / (2 * 2.0^2)) + 1, stage = "After repeated exposure")
)
pts <- data.frame(novelty = runif(120, 0, 10),
                  stage = rep(c("First encounter", "After repeated exposure"), each = 60)) |>
  mutate(mu = ifelse(stage == "First encounter",
                     6 * exp(-(novelty - 3.8)^2 / (2 * 1.9^2)) + 1,
                     6 * exp(-(novelty - 6.0)^2 / (2 * 2.0^2)) + 1),
         liking = mu + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.6))
ggplot(curve_df, aes(novelty, liking, colour = stage)) +
  geom_point(data = pts, alpha = 0.35, size = 1.6) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.3, y = 0.3, label = "Too familiar:\nboring", hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 9.7, y = 0.3, label = "Too novel:\nunsettling", hjust = 1, size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("First encounter" = pal[["blue"]], "After repeated exposure" = pal[["orange"]]),
                      breaks = c("First encounter", "After repeated exposure")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.5, 8.5)) +
  labs(x = "Novelty / complexity of the stimulus", y = "Liking", colour = NULL,
       title = "Liking peaks at moderate novelty, and the peak moves",
       caption = "Illustrative: Gaussian-shaped curves with simulated ratings (n = 60 per stage).")
```

::: {.debate}
**Inverted-U or monotonic typicality?** Berlyne's framework predicts that
moderately novel or complex stimuli are preferred. Yet studies by Martindale and
colleagues found that **typicality**, how representative a stimulus is of its
category, often predicted aesthetic preference better than novelty or complexity,
a result they described as anomalous for Berlyne's theory [@martindale1988;
@martindale1990]. The finding links directly to the
[beauty-in-averageness](#beauty-in-averageness) effect. One reconciliation is that
typicality and novelty are not opposite ends of one dimension: a design can be both
recognisably typical and fresh in its details. @hekkert2003 found that typicality
and novelty were *both* positively related to preference for industrial designs
once their negative correlation with each other was taken into account: the
"most advanced, yet acceptable" principle. For researchers, the lesson is to
measure typicality and novelty separately rather than assuming they are mirror
images.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Product design and innovation newness.** Firms launching new products face a
Goldilocks trade-off. A design that is too close to existing products fails to
attract attention or justify a premium. A design that is too radical can confuse
consumers and depress adoption until the market catches up. Automotive design is a
frequently discussed case: manufacturers typically evolve the appearance of
established models gradually, preserving recognisable cues while refreshing
details, and reserve radical departures for concept cars that test consumer
reactions. The inverted-U also implies that the optimal level of novelty differs by
segment. Experts and enthusiasts, who have seen many variants, tend to prefer
higher novelty than novices, so a product line may include a mainstream variant for
the broad market and a more adventurous variant for enthusiasts.
:::

## Coolidge Effect {#coolidge-effect}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** In many mammalian species, a male that has reached sexual satiety
with one partner shows renewed sexual behaviour when a novel receptive partner is
introduced.

**Origins.** Comparative psychology, @wilson1963, reviewed by @dewsbury1981, the
name refers to an anecdote about US President Calvin Coolidge reported in
@Johnson_1972.

**Level of analysis.** Individual organism.

**Key constructs.** Sexual satiety, stimulus novelty, recovery of responding.

**Boundary conditions.** Documented primarily in non-human animals. The extent and
form of the effect vary across species and between sexes. Applications to human
consumption are **analogies**, not direct applications.

**Related theories.** [Goldilocks effect](#goldilocks-effect),
[Hedonic adaptation](#hedonic-adaptation), [Mere exposure](#mere-exposure-effect).
:::

The name comes from a story that has been retold many times. As reported by
@Johnson_1972:

> "... The President and Mrs. Coolidge were being shown (separately) around an
> experimental government farm. When [Mrs. Coolidge] came to the chicken yard she
> noticed that a rooster was mating very frequently. She asked the attendant how
> often that happened and was told, 'Dozens of times each day.' Mrs. Coolidge said,
> 'Tell that to the President when he comes by.' Upon being told, the President
> asked, 'Same hen every time?' The reply was, 'Oh, no, Mr. President, a different
> hen every time.' President: 'Tell that to Mrs. Coolidge.'"

The anecdote is almost certainly apocryphal, but the phenomenon is well documented.
@wilson1963 showed that male rats that had stopped copulating with one female
resumed sexual activity when a new female was introduced. @dewsbury1981 reviewed
evidence across many species, showing that novelty effects on copulatory behaviour
are widespread but vary in form. Effects in females have been studied less and
appear in some species but are generally weaker or different in form.

### The business analogue: satiation and variety seeking

The underlying principle, that responding to a stimulus declines with repetition
and recovers when the stimulus changes, has close parallels in consumer behaviour
that do not depend on any claim about sexuality. **Sensory-specific satiety** is
the decline in the pleasantness of a food as it is eaten, relative to foods that
have not been eaten. @rolls1981 showed that the decline is specific to the eaten
food, which helps explain why people eat more when offered variety. **Variety
seeking**, switching among options for the sake of change, has been studied
extensively in marketing [@mcalister1982]. @ratner1999 found that people sometimes
choose less-preferred items for the sake of variety, and that this can reduce
moment-to-moment enjoyment even when people remember the varied sequence
favourably.

::: {.business-case}
**Novelty in product lines.** Food and beverage companies, quick-service
restaurants, and consumer-goods firms manage satiation through rotating flavours,
limited-time offers, and seasonal menus. These tactics address a real problem:
consumers who are satiated on one variant may switch brands rather than stop buying
the category. Offering variety *within* the brand captures that switching. Media
and entertainment platforms do the same through recommendation algorithms that
balance familiar content with new content. The research also warns of costs:
excessive variety increases complexity and inventory costs, and, as
@ratner1999 suggest, variety chosen for its own sake does not always improve
experienced satisfaction.
:::

## Bandwagon, Snob, and Veblen Effects {#snob-effect}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** An individual's demand for a good can depend on how many others
consume it and on its price as such. Under a **bandwagon effect**, demand rises
because others consume the good. Under a **snob effect**, demand falls because
others consume it. Under a **Veblen effect**, demand rises with the price itself,
because a high price displays wealth.

**Origins.** Economics, @Leibenstein_1950, building on @veblen1899, extended in
@bagwell1996.

**Level of analysis.** Individual consumer and market demand.

**Key constructs.** Functional versus non-functional demand, external
consumption effects, conspicuous price, exclusivity, status.

**Boundary conditions.** Requires that consumption be observable or that its price
be known to relevant others. Strongest for status goods, fashion, and goods whose
value depends on network size.

**Related theories.** [Costly signaling](#costly-signaling),
[Identity signaling](#identity-signaling), [Countersignaling](#countersignaling),
[Optimal distinctiveness](#optimal-distinctiveness-theory).
:::

### Core logic

Standard demand theory assumes that a consumer's demand for a good depends on its
price, the consumer's income, and the prices of other goods, but not on what other
people buy. @Leibenstein_1950 relaxed that assumption. He distinguished
**functional** demand, which depends on the qualities inherent in the good, from
**non-functional** demand arising from external effects on utility. Among the
latter, he identified three:

```{r tab-eff-leibenstein}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Effect, ~`Demand depends on`, ~`Direction`, ~`Consequence for market demand`, ~`Business example`,
  "Bandwagon", "Number of others consuming", "Positive: more adopters, more demand", "Demand is more price-elastic than functional demand", "Fashion trends, social platforms, best-seller lists",
  "Snob", "Number of others consuming", "Negative: more adopters, less demand", "Demand is less price-elastic than functional demand", "Limited editions, niche luxury, exclusive clubs",
  "Veblen", "Price itself (conspicuous price)", "Positive: higher price, more demand over some range", "Demand curve can slope upward over a range", "Prestige watches, luxury handbags, premium spirits"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Leibenstein's (1950) three external effects on demand.")
```

The snob effect connects to the identity-signaling literature reviewed in Chapter
\@ref(information): people avoid goods that have become too common because the goods
no longer signal distinction [@Berger_2007]. The Veblen effect connects to costly
signaling: a good whose price is high and known can function as a credible display
of wealth [@veblen1899; @bagwell1996]. When many people adopt a status good,
early adopters may abandon it, and marketers respond by cultivating an *illusion
of distinction*: emphasising the ways in which offerings differ, even when they
are similar at the core. Figure
\@ref(fig:fig-eff-demand) sketches the implications for demand curves.

```{r fig-eff-demand, fig.cap = "Stylised market demand curves. Relative to functional demand, a bandwagon effect makes demand more price-elastic, a snob effect makes it less elastic, and a Veblen effect can produce an upward-sloping segment over a range of prices. All curves pass through a common point for comparison.", fig.height = 4.2}
p <- seq(20, 80, by = 1)
dem <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(price = p, qty = 50 - (p - 50), curve = "Functional demand"),
  data.frame(price = p, qty = 50 - 1.8 * (p - 50), curve = "Bandwagon"),
  data.frame(price = p, qty = 50 - 0.45 * (p - 50), curve = "Snob"),
  data.frame(price = p, qty = 50 + 0.6 * (p - 50), curve = "Veblen (over this range)")
) |>
  filter(qty >= 0, qty <= 100) |>
  mutate(curve = factor(curve, levels = c("Functional demand", "Bandwagon", "Snob", "Veblen (over this range)")))
labs_df <- tibble::tribble(
  ~qty, ~price, ~curve, ~hj,
  81, 20, "Functional demand", 0,
  99.5, 23, "Bandwagon", 0,
  35.5, 80, "Snob", 1,
  69.5, 80, "Veblen (over this range)", 0
)
ggplot(dem, aes(qty, price, colour = curve)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.05) +
  geom_text(data = labs_df, aes(label = curve, hjust = hj), size = 3.2,
            colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(pal[["blue"]], pal[["orange"]], pal[["aqua"]], pal[["yellow"]]), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 115)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(15, 90)) +
  labs(x = "Quantity demanded", y = "Price",
       title = "Social and price effects change the shape of demand",
       caption = "Stylised linear curves for illustration, not estimated from data.")
```

::: {.business-case}
**Luxury scarcity versus mass adoption.** Luxury houses manage the snob and Veblen
effects deliberately. They restrict distribution to owned boutiques and selected
retailers, limit production of iconic items, avoid frequent discounting, and
sometimes allocate the most desirable products to established clients rather than
selling them to anyone who walks in. Each practice preserves exclusivity and keeps
price conspicuous. The tension with growth is real: expanding into accessible
"masstige" lines, outlet stores, or heavy discounting can attract new customers
while diluting the brand's value to existing ones. The controversy in 2018, when
Burberry disclosed that it had been destroying unsold stock to protect its brand and
then announced it would end the practice, illustrates the costs of defending
exclusivity in an era of sustainability scrutiny. By contrast, products with strong
**bandwagon** or network effects, social platforms, messaging apps, marketplaces,
benefit from rapid mass adoption, and their managers subsidise early users to reach
critical mass. Diagnosing which effect dominates in a category is therefore a
strategic decision with opposite implications for pricing and distribution.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Mistaking a quality inference for a Veblen effect.** Demand that rises with price
is not necessarily a Veblen effect. Consumers may infer *quality* from price when
quality is hard to observe, which is an information effect (see
[Signaling theory](#signaling-theory)), not a desire to display price to others.
Distinguishing the two requires variation in observability: a Veblen effect should
be stronger for publicly consumed goods, whereas price-quality inference should
operate for private goods as well.
:::

## Glass Cliff Effect {#glass-cliff-effect}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Women, and, in later research, members of racial and ethnic
minority groups, are more likely than white men to be appointed to leadership
positions that are **precarious**: roles in organisations that are performing poorly
or are in crisis, where the risk of failure and criticism is high.

**Origins.** Organisational and social psychology, @Ryan_2005, reviewed in
@Ryan_2016 and meta-analysed in @morgenroth2020.

**Level of analysis.** Individual appointment decisions within organisations, board
and organisational level.

**Key constructs.** Precariousness (prior performance, crisis), leader gender and
ethnicity, leadership stereotypes ("think manager-think male", "think crisis-think
female"), signalling change, scapegoating.

**Boundary conditions.** Depends on how precariousness is measured (share-price
versus accounting performance), on the history of leadership in the organisation,
and on the country and industry context.

**Related theories.** [Upper echelons theory](#upper-echelons-theory),
[Social identity theory](#social-identity-theory), [Signaling](#signaling-theory),
[Agency theory](#agency-theory).
:::

### Origins and evidence

The glass cliff was identified as a response to a public claim. In 2003, a
newspaper article argued that companies with more women on their boards performed
worse. @Ryan_2005 examined the timing of board appointments in FTSE 100 companies
and found the reverse causal story: companies that appointed women to their boards
had typically experienced consistently poor share-price performance in the months
*before* the appointment, whereas companies that appointed men had relatively
stable performance. Women were not causing poor performance. They were more likely
to be appointed when performance was already poor. The authors coined the term
**glass cliff** to complement the familiar "glass ceiling": even when women break
through to leadership, they may be placed in positions where failure is more likely.

Subsequent research, reviewed in @Ryan_2016, used both archival and experimental
designs. In experiments, participants, including business and law students and
managers, choose between equally qualified male and female candidates for a
leadership role or high-risk assignment that is described as either going well or
going badly. Female candidates are more often chosen when the situation is
described as precarious. @ryan2011 found that the stereotype of the ideal manager
shifts in crisis: people associate the characteristics needed to manage a failing
company with stereotypically female traits more than they do for a successful
company ("think crisis-think female"). @bruckmuller2010 found that preference for a
female leader in crisis depended on the organisation's leadership history: when a
company had been led by men, a crisis increased the preference for a woman, in part
because appointing a woman signalled change.

The pattern is not limited to gender. Studying chief executives of Fortune 500
firms, @cook2014 found that women and racial and ethnic minorities were more likely
than white men to be promoted to CEO of weakly performing firms, and that when firm
performance declined during their tenure, they were more likely to be replaced by
white men: a pattern the authors described as a "saviour effect".

```{r fig-eff-glasscliff, fig.cap = "Mechanisms proposed for the glass cliff. Organisational precariousness activates beliefs about what a crisis requires and a desire to signal change. These shape appointments of women and minorities to risky roles, whose higher failure risk can feed back into stereotypes about their leadership."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  P  [label = "Precarious context\\n(poor performance, crisis)", %s]
  S  [label = "Think crisis-think female:\\nstereotype fit to crisis", %s]
  C  [label = "Desire to signal\\nchange", %s]
  N  [label = "Limited alternative\\nopportunities, weaker\\nnetwork protection", %s]
  A  [label = "Appointment of a woman\\nor minority leader\\nto a risky role", %s]
  F  [label = "Higher risk of failure\\nand blame", %s]
  H  [label = "History of male\\nleadership", %s]
  P -> S -> A
  P -> C -> A
  N -> A
  A -> F
  F -> S [style = dashed, label = " reinforces\\n stereotypes", constraint = false]
  H -> C [style = dashed]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_outcome,
   node_outcome, node_moderator))
```

```{r tab-eff-glasscliff}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Explanation, ~`Core argument`, ~`Representative evidence`,
  "Think crisis-think female", "Stereotypically female traits are seen as fitting crisis management", "Ryan et al. (2011)",
  "Signalling change", "Appointing a non-traditional leader signals that the organisation is changing course", "Bruckmuller & Branscombe (2010)",
  "Scapegoating", "Leaders appointed in crisis can be blamed if recovery fails", "Discussed in Ryan et al. (2016)",
  "Limited alternatives", "Candidates with fewer opportunities may accept riskier roles", "Discussed in Ryan et al. (2016)",
  "In-group protection", "Decision makers shield members of their own group from risky roles", "Discussed in Ryan et al. (2016)",
  "Saviour effect", "Minority leaders are replaced by white men when performance declines", "Cook & Glass (2014)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Explanations for the glass cliff.")
```

::: {.debate}
**How general is the glass cliff?** Archival evidence is sensitive to measurement
choices. Using US data and several performance measures, @adams2009 did not find
that female executives were systematically appointed to firms with poorer prior
performance, suggesting that the original pattern might depend on the performance
measure, the market, or the period. Experimental evidence is more consistent, but
experiments abstract from real selection processes. A meta-analysis by
@morgenroth2020 found evidence for the glass cliff while documenting substantial
variation across study designs, samples, and contexts. A balanced reading is that
the glass cliff is a real tendency whose strength depends on context: in
particular, on the organisation's leadership history and on how precariousness is
defined and observed by decision makers.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Leadership appointments in crisis firms.** Consider an *illustrative scenario*:
a retailer's board must replace a chief executive after a year of falling sales and
a data breach. The board's shortlist contains an internal female executive and an
external male candidate. Glass cliff research does not say which candidate to
choose. It identifies risks in how the decision is made and implemented. First,
boards should ask whether the appointment is driven by a desire to *signal* change
rather than by an assessment of fit, because signalling motives can coexist with
under-investment in the new leader's success. Second, boards should equip leaders
appointed to turnarounds with the resources a turnaround requires, authority to
restructure, board support, time, and set performance expectations that reflect
the starting position rather than the industry average. Third, evaluation should be
benchmarked against the counterfactual trajectory of the firm, so that a leader who
slows a decline is not judged a failure. These practices protect the firm as well as
the leader: an under-supported turnaround is costly regardless of who leads it.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* The probability that a newly appointed CEO is a woman increases with the
  firm's negative performance in the preceding year.
- *H2.* This relationship is stronger for firms with a history of exclusively male
  leadership [@bruckmuller2010].
- *H3.* Conditional on performance during tenure, women and minority CEOs face a
  higher hazard of dismissal than white male CEOs [@cook2014].

**Designs.** Archival panels of executive and board appointments with lagged
performance measures. Event-history models of tenure. Vignette experiments
manipulating precariousness and leadership history.

**Measures.** Prior share-price and accounting performance, analyst downgrades,
crisis events, leader demographics, tenure and exit.
:::

## IKEA Effect {#ikea-effect}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** People value products that they have created or assembled
themselves more than equivalent products created by others: labour leads to love.

**Origins.** Consumer psychology, @norton2012, related to the "I designed it
myself" effect in mass customisation [@franke2010] and to effort justification
[@aronson1959].

**Level of analysis.** Individual consumer.

**Key constructs.** Self-created product, labour or effort, task completion,
feelings of competence and accomplishment, willingness to pay.

**Boundary conditions.** The effect depends on **successful completion**. It
disappears when people fail to complete the task or when their creation is
destroyed, and very frustrating tasks may reduce rather than increase valuation.

**Related theories.** [Endowment effect](#endowment-effect),
[Self-determination theory](#self-determination-theory),
[Decoy effect](#decoy-effect) (another lever in product-line design).
:::

### Core logic and evidence

@norton2012 named the effect after the Swedish furniture retailer whose flat-pack
products require customers to assemble them. In their experiments, participants who
assembled a simple storage box were willing to pay more for it than participants who
inspected an identical, pre-assembled box. Participants who folded origami valued
their own amateur creations far above how other people valued them, and close to the
value they placed on origami made by experts, and they expected others to share
their valuation. Crucially, the effect depended on completion: when participants
built and then destroyed their creations, or did not complete them, the increase in
valuation disappeared.

The effect has three candidate mechanisms that are not mutually exclusive. The
first is **effort justification**: people value outcomes for which they have
suffered, as in the classic finding that a severe initiation increased liking for a
group [@aronson1959]. The second is **competence**: successfully completing a task
signals to oneself that one is capable, and the product becomes a symbol of that
competence. The third is **ownership and self-extension**: a self-made product is
more closely linked to the self, which connects the IKEA effect to the
[endowment effect](#endowment-effect). @franke2010 found a related pattern in mass
customisation: consumers were willing to pay more for products they had designed
themselves, beyond what the better fit to their preferences could explain, and this
"I designed it myself" effect was associated with a feeling of accomplishment.

```{r fig-eff-ikea, fig.cap = "Mechanism of the IKEA effect. Labour that culminates in successful completion produces feelings of competence and ownership, which raise the creator's valuation. Failure to complete eliminates the effect (Norton, Mochon, & Ariely, 2012)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  L  [label = "Labour invested\\n(assembly, design,\\ncustomisation)", %s]
  C  [label = "Successful\\ncompletion", %s]
  M1 [label = "Feelings of competence\\nand accomplishment", %s]
  M2 [label = "Ownership and\\nself-extension", %s]
  M3 [label = "Effort\\njustification", %s]
  V  [label = "Higher valuation and\\nwillingness to pay", %s]
  D  [label = "Task difficulty\\n(too hard = frustration)", %s]
  L -> C
  C -> M1 -> V
  C -> M2 -> V
  L -> M3 -> V
  D -> C [style = dashed]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_mechanism,
   node_outcome, node_moderator))
```

::: {.business-case}
**Co-creation and self-assembly products.** The IKEA effect is visible in many
business models that ask customers to do part of the work: flat-pack furniture,
meal kits that require cooking, build-your-own toys, and online configurators for
shoes, computers, and cars. The research suggests three design principles. First,
**calibrate effort**: the task must be demanding enough to feel like an
accomplishment but easy enough to complete. Instructions, pre-drilled parts, and
modular design reduce the risk of failure that would eliminate the effect. Second,
**make completion visible**: a finished product, a shareable design, or a
personalised element ensures that the customer's contribution is salient. Third,
**beware the creator's bias**: just as participants expected others to value their
origami, customers and employees overvalue their own creations. In product
development, this means that teams can become attached to features they built.
In co-creation programmes, it means that participants' enthusiasm is not a reliable
guide to the market's.
:::

## Decoy Effect {#decoy-effect}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Adding an option that is clearly inferior to one existing option
(the **target**) but not to another (the **competitor**) increases the share of
choices going to the target. The effect is also called the **attraction effect** or
**asymmetric dominance effect**.

**Origins.** Consumer research, @huber1982, extended by @simonson1989 and
@simonson1992, robustness debated in a 2014 *Journal of Marketing Research*
exchange [@frederick2014; @huber2014; @yang2014].

**Level of analysis.** Individual choice, market shares.

**Key constructs.** Target, competitor, decoy, asymmetric dominance, regularity,
compromise effect, justification.

**Boundary conditions.** Strongest when options are described by a small number of
numeric attributes, when the dominance relation is easy to see, and when people
expect to justify their choice. Weak or absent with perceptual or holistic stimuli.

**Related theories.** [Screening theory](#screening-theory),
[Heuristics and biases](#heuristics-biases), [Anchoring](#anchoring-effect),
[Prospect theory](#prospect-theory).
:::

### Core logic

Most models of rational choice imply **regularity**: adding a new option to a choice
set cannot increase the probability of choosing any option already in the set. The
new option can only take share away. @huber1982 showed that this principle can be
violated. When they added an option that was dominated by one alternative (worse on
both attributes) but not by the other, the share of the dominating alternative
increased. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-eff-decoy) illustrates the geometry: the decoy sits
in the region that the target dominates but the competitor does not.

```{r fig-eff-decoy, fig.cap = "Stylised attribute space for the decoy effect. The decoy (D) is worse than the target (T) on both quality and affordability but is not dominated by the competitor (C). Its presence makes T look better by comparison. Positions are illustrative.", fig.height = 4.4}
opts <- tibble::tribble(
  ~option, ~quality, ~afford, ~role,
  "T: Target", 75, 40, "Target",
  "C: Competitor", 40, 75, "Competitor",
  "D: Decoy", 66, 30, "Decoy"
)
ggplot(opts, aes(quality, afford)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 40, xmax = 75, ymin = 0, ymax = 40, fill = pal[["orange"]], alpha = 0.10) +
  annotate("segment", x = 40, xend = 75, y = 75, yend = 40, colour = ink[["muted"]], linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = role), size = 4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = option), nudge_x = 2.2, hjust = 0, size = 3.5, colour = ink[["primary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 57.5, y = 8, label = "Region dominated by T\nbut not by C (asymmetric dominance)",
           size = 3.1, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 61, y = 66, label = "Trade-off line:\nT and C equally attractive", size = 3.1,
           colour = ink[["secondary"]], hjust = 0) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Target = pal[["blue"]], Competitor = pal[["aqua"]], Decoy = pal[["orange"]]), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(20, 100)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 90)) +
  labs(x = "Quality (higher is better)", y = "Affordability (higher is better)",
       title = "Where a decoy sits",
       caption = "Stylised positions for illustration.")
```

Several context effects are related. The **compromise effect** describes the
tendency for an option to gain share when it becomes the intermediate option in a
set, because extreme options are less attractive than moderate ones: an aspect of
**extremeness aversion** [@simonson1992]. @simonson1989 proposed that both
attraction and compromise effects reflect **choice based on reasons**: a dominated
decoy gives the chooser an easy justification for the target ("it is clearly better
than D"), and the effects are stronger when people expect to be evaluated on their
choice. Table \@ref(tab:tab-eff-decoy) summarises the main variants.

```{r tab-eff-decoy}
tibble::tribble(
  ~`Context effect`, ~`Position of the added option`, ~`Predicted shift`, ~`Proposed mechanism`, ~`Key source`,
  "Attraction (asymmetric dominance)", "Dominated by the target only", "Toward the target", "Dominance provides a reason, relative advantage", "Huber, Payne & Puto (1982)",
  "Compromise", "Makes the target the middle option", "Toward the middle option", "Extremeness aversion, ease of justification", "Simonson (1989), Simonson & Tversky (1992)",
  "Similarity (substitution)", "Very similar to one existing option", "Away from the similar option", "New option draws share from close substitutes", "Discussed in Huber, Payne & Puto (1982)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Context effects in multi-attribute choice.")
```

::: {.debate}
**How robust is the attraction effect?** @frederick2014 reported a series of studies
in which the attraction effect was frequently absent when options were described
perceptually or qualitatively, for example, with pictures rather than numeric
tables, and in some studies the effect reversed. They argued that the effect is
much narrower than the literature implied. @yang2014 likewise reported difficulty
obtaining the effect with realistic stimuli. In reply, @huber2014 accepted that the
effect has limits but argued that it is robust where its conditions are met: when
decision makers recognise the dominance relation, when attributes are commensurable,
and when the decoy is plausible rather than absurd. The exchange is a model of
productive debate. It moved the field from asking *whether* the effect exists to
asking *when* it occurs, and it cautions practitioners against assuming that a
decoy that worked in a numeric laboratory task will work in a visually rich
storefront.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Pricing tiers and decoys.** Subscription and software pricing pages commonly
present three or four plans. Some plans may exist primarily to shape choice among the
others. @ariely2008 popularised the example of a magazine subscription offer that
included a print-only option priced the same as a combined print-and-web option.
Few would choose print-only, but its presence made the combined offer look like a
bargain, and removing it shifted choices toward the cheaper web-only option in his
classroom demonstrations. Restaurants use a similar logic when an expensive wine on
the menu makes the second-most-expensive bottle look reasonable, and cinemas when a
medium popcorn is priced close to the large. The decoy literature suggests guidelines
for practice: decoys work best when the comparison with the target is easy to
see (shared attributes, numeric presentation, adjacent placement), when customers
are comparing rather than choosing by gut feeling, and when the decoy is credible. It
also suggests caution. Customers who recognise a decoy as manipulative may lose
trust (see the [persuasion knowledge model](#persuasion-knowledge-model)), and a
decoy that customers actually choose is simply a poorly priced product.
:::

::: {.try-it}
Find a pricing page for a subscription service with at least three tiers. For each
pair of tiers, ask whether one dominates the other on price and features. Is any
tier asymmetrically dominated? Is any tier positioned as a compromise? Predict how
choice shares would change if that tier were removed.
:::

## Anchoring Effect {#anchoring-effect}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Numeric estimates are biased toward a value that was considered
beforehand, the **anchor**, even when the anchor is obviously irrelevant.

**Origins.** Judgment and decision making, @tversky1974, extended to valuation by
@ariely2003, reviewed by @furnham2011.

**Level of analysis.** Individual judgment, dyadic negotiation.

**Key constructs.** Anchor (externally provided or self-generated), adjustment,
selective accessibility, plausibility of the anchor.

**Boundary conditions.** Robust across domains and expertise levels. Effects are
larger when the target quantity is uncertain and the anchor is plausible, and can be
reduced by generating reasons why the anchor is inappropriate.

**Related theories.** [Heuristics and biases](#heuristics-biases),
[Framing](#framing-theory), [Decoy effect](#decoy-effect),
[Prospect theory](#prospect-theory).
:::

### Core logic and evidence

In the best-known demonstration, @tversky1974 spun a wheel of fortune that was
rigged to stop at either 10 or 65 in front of participants, who then estimated the
percentage of African countries in the United Nations. The arbitrary number
influenced the estimates: median estimates were 25 among participants who saw 10 and
45 among those who saw 65 (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-eff-anchoring)). Tversky and
Kahneman attributed the effect to **insufficient adjustment**: people start from the
anchor and adjust toward a plausible value, but stop too soon.

```{r fig-eff-anchoring, fig.cap = "Anchoring with an arbitrary number. Median estimates of the percentage of African countries in the United Nations after participants saw a wheel of fortune stop at 10 or 65, as reported by Tversky & Kahneman (1974).", fig.height = 3}
anch <- tibble::tribble(
  ~condition, ~anchor, ~estimate,
  "Low anchor", 10, 25,
  "High anchor", 65, 45
) |>
  mutate(condition = factor(condition, levels = c("High anchor", "Low anchor")))
ggplot(anch, aes(y = condition)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = anchor, xend = estimate, yend = condition), colour = ink[["muted"]],
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm")), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(x = anchor, colour = "Anchor shown"), size = 3.4) +
  geom_point(aes(x = estimate, colour = "Median estimate"), size = 3.4) +
  geom_text(aes(x = anchor, label = anchor), vjust = -1.1, size = 3.3, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  geom_text(aes(x = estimate, label = estimate), vjust = -1.1, size = 3.3, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Anchor shown" = pal[["orange"]], "Median estimate" = pal[["blue"]])) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 75)) +
  labs(x = "Percentage of African countries in the UN", y = NULL, colour = NULL,
       title = "An arbitrary number pulls estimates toward it",
       caption = "Source: medians reported in Tversky & Kahneman (1974).")
```

Anchoring extends to valuation. @ariely2003 asked participants to write down the last
two digits of their social security number and to state whether they would pay that
amount, in dollars, for various products such as wine and computer accessories.
Participants then stated their maximum willingness to pay. Valuations were strongly
correlated with the arbitrary digits. Yet the *relative* valuations of different
products were sensible: participants valued items that should be worth more at
higher prices. The authors described this pattern as **coherent arbitrariness**:
preferences are internally consistent but anchored to arbitrary starting points.

Expertise does not eliminate anchoring. @northcraft1987 gave real estate agents and
amateurs identical information about a house, varying only the listing price. Both
groups' appraisals were influenced by the listing price, and the agents tended to deny
that it had influenced them. In negotiations, **first offers** act as anchors:
@galinsky2001 found that the party making the first offer tended to obtain better
outcomes, and that the effect was reduced when the recipient focused on information
inconsistent with the anchor, such as the offerer's alternatives.

### Mechanism

Two mechanisms have been proposed, and they appear to apply to different kinds of
anchors. The **adjustment** account fits **self-generated** anchors: values people
produce themselves as starting points, such as the known boiling point of water when
estimating it at altitude. @epley2006 found that people adjust from such anchors
until they reach a plausible value and then stop, producing estimates biased toward
the anchor. The **selective accessibility** account fits **externally provided**
anchors. @strack1997 argued that considering whether the target quantity is higher or
lower than the anchor makes anchor-consistent information more accessible, and that
this information then shapes the final estimate. Anchoring is also among the most
replicable effects in psychology: it replicated robustly in the multi-laboratory
Many Labs project [@klein2014].

```{r tab-eff-anchoring}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Paradigm, ~`Anchor type`, ~`Typical finding`, ~`Business setting`, ~Source,
  "Wheel of fortune", "Arbitrary, externally provided", "Estimates move toward the random number", "Survey and forecasting design", "Tversky & Kahneman (1974)",
  "Social security digits", "Arbitrary, self-relevant", "Willingness to pay tracks the digits (coherent arbitrariness)", "Reference prices, price recommendations", "Ariely, Loewenstein & Prelec (2003)",
  "Listing price", "Informative but biased", "Expert appraisals follow the listing price", "Real estate, procurement", "Northcraft & Neale (1987)",
  "First offer", "Strategic, from counterpart", "First mover obtains better outcomes", "Negotiation, salary setting", "Galinsky & Mussweiler (2001)",
  "Self-generated", "Known value adjusted from", "Adjustment stops too early", "Budgeting from last year's figures", "Epley & Gilovich (2006)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Anchoring paradigms and their business counterparts.")
```

::: {.business-case}
**Reference prices and negotiation.** Retailers display "was" prices, manufacturers
publish suggested retail prices, and software firms list an annual price beside a
discounted monthly equivalent. Each provides an anchor against which the actual
price is judged. Regulators in many jurisdictions restrict fictitious reference
prices precisely because anchors influence perceived value. In business-to-business
negotiation, the anchoring literature recommends that well-prepared parties consider
making the first offer, and that recipients of an aggressive first offer counter its
influence by focusing on their own alternatives and target rather than on the
counterpart's number [@galinsky2001]. Inside organisations, last year's budget is a
self-generated anchor. Zero-based budgeting is, in part, an attempt to remove it.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Treating every reference point as an anchor.** A displayed price can affect
judgments because it is an anchor, because it is *informative* (a high list price
may truthfully signal quality), or because it changes the reference point against
which gains and losses are evaluated ([Prospect theory](#prospect-theory)).
Demonstrating anchoring requires showing that an uninformative or randomly assigned
number shifts judgments.
:::

## Beauty in Averageness {#beauty-in-averageness}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Stimuli that are close to the average or prototype of their category
, faces, designs, musical performances, tend to be judged attractive.

**Origins.** Perception and evolutionary psychology, @langlois1990, extended to
non-face categories by @halberstadt2003 and to products by @veryzerjr.1998 and
@landwehr2011.

**Level of analysis.** Individual perceiver.

**Key constructs.** Averageness, prototypicality (typicality), symmetry, processing
fluency, aesthetic preference.

**Boundary conditions.** Averageness is attractive but not maximally attractive:
some non-average features can be preferred, and in some categories distinctiveness
adds value. The effect is weaker when typicality is confounded with boredom.

**Related theories.** [Goldilocks effect](#goldilocks-effect),
[Processing fluency](#processing-fluency), [Mere exposure](#mere-exposure-effect),
[Wisdom of the crowd](#wisdom-of-the-crowd).
:::

### Core logic and evidence

@langlois1990 created composite faces by digitally averaging photographs of
individuals. Composite faces were judged more attractive than most of the individual
faces from which they were created, and attractiveness tended to increase as more
faces were included in the composite (see also @strzalko1992 on how attractiveness
assessments vary within and between raters). The pattern is
not specific to faces. @halberstadt2003 found that computer-averaged images of birds,
fish, and automobiles were also judged attractive. In music, @repp1997 found that a
performance constructed by averaging the expressive timing and dynamics of many
pianists' performances was judged aesthetically pleasing: in some respects more so
than most individual performances. In experimental aesthetics, Martindale and
colleagues found that typicality was a strong predictor of preference for many kinds
of stimuli [@martindale1988; @martindale1990].

The effect has clear business relevance. @veryzerjr.1998 found that prototypicality
and unity increased aesthetic responses to new product designs. @landwehr2011
showed that a measure of **design fluency**, capturing how typical and how complex a
car's design was, improved forecasts of automobile sales beyond conventional
predictors, suggesting that the ease with which consumers process a design is
commercially consequential.

### Explanations

Three families of explanation have been proposed, summarised in Table
\@ref(tab:tab-eff-averageness).

```{r tab-eff-averageness}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Explanation, ~`Core argument`, ~`Key sources`, ~`Prediction that distinguishes it`,
  "Evolutionary (good genes)", "Average and symmetric faces signal developmental stability and genetic diversity", "Thornhill & Gangestad (1993), Grammer & Thornhill (1994), Langlois & Roggman (1990), Rhodes (2006)", "Effect should be strongest for faces and mates",
  "Processing fluency", "Prototypes are easy to process, and ease is experienced as pleasure", "Winkielman et al. (2006), Reber (2011), Reber, Schwarz & Winkielman (2004), Landwehr et al. (2011)", "Effect should extend to any category with a prototype, including novel ones",
  "Wisdom of crowds (error cancellation)", "Averaging cancels idiosyncratic deviations, moving the result closer to an optimum", "Surowiecki (2005), Halberstadt & Rhodes (2003), Repp (1997)", "Averages of skilled performances should beat most individuals"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Three explanations for beauty in averageness.")
```

The **evolutionary** account holds that averageness and symmetry in faces are cues to
health and genetic quality, so preferences for them would have been favoured by
selection [@thornhill1993; @grammer1994; @rhodes2006]. The **fluency** account holds
that prototypes are processed easily, and that the resulting fluency is experienced as
positive affect. @winkielman2006 found that prototypical patterns were classified
faster and liked more, consistent with fluency, and @reber2011 develops the argument
that fluency underlies culturally shared taste. Because the fluency account predicts
the effect for any category with a prototype, including categories with no
evolutionary significance, such as cars or dot patterns, findings such as those of
@halberstadt2003 are often read as favouring it. The **wisdom-of-crowds** account
draws on the statistical point that averaging independent estimates cancels their
errors [@surowiecki2005wisdom]: an averaged face or performance smooths out
idiosyncratic deviations, moving the result toward an optimum
[@halberstadt2003; @repp1997].

::: {.business-case}
**Typicality in product design.** The beauty-in-averageness effect explains why many
successful designs look "right" at first sight: they are close to the category
prototype. It also explains a frequent tension between designers, who value
originality, and market research, which often favours familiar forms. The
[Goldilocks effect](#goldilocks-effect) and the "most advanced, yet acceptable"
principle suggest a resolution: keep the overall form typical, the silhouette of a
car, the layout of a website, the shape of a bottle, and innovate in details that
distinguish the brand. @landwehr2011's results suggest that design properties such
as typicality and complexity can be measured during development and used to forecast sales, allowing firms to treat
design not purely as a matter of taste but as a measurable predictor of market
performance.
:::

## Pratfall Effect {#pratfall-effect}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** A minor blunder can make a highly competent person more likeable,
whereas the same blunder makes a person of average competence less likeable.

**Origins.** Social psychology, @aronson1966, qualified by @helmreich1970.

**Level of analysis.** Individual perceiver evaluating a target person (and, by
extension, a brand).

**Key constructs.** Competence, blunder (pratfall), likeability, perceiver
self-esteem, blemishing.

**Boundary conditions.** Requires that the target's competence already be
established and that the blunder be minor and unrelated to core competence. Effects
depend on characteristics of the perceiver.

**Related theories.** [Persuasion knowledge model](#persuasion-knowledge-model),
[Social comparison theory](#social-comparison-theory),
[Signaling theory](#signaling-theory).
:::

@aronson1966 had participants listen to a tape recording of a student who was
supposedly trying out for a college quiz team. In one version, the candidate answered
almost all questions correctly and described an impressive record. In another, he
performed at an average level. In half of the recordings, the candidate clumsily
spilled coffee over himself near the end. The blunder *increased* the attractiveness
of the superior candidate and *decreased* the attractiveness of the average
candidate. The interpretation was that a minor flaw makes a highly competent person
seem more human and approachable, whereas for a person of average ability it simply
adds to an impression of mediocrity.

The effect is less general than its popularity suggests. @helmreich1970 found that
the effect of a pratfall depended on the self-esteem of the observer, so that the
blundering superior person was not uniformly preferred. Related research in consumer
behaviour points to a broader principle. @eingar2012 documented a **blemishing
effect**: adding a small piece of negative information to an otherwise positive
description of a product can *increase* evaluations, especially when people process
information with little effort, because the weak negative information makes the
positive information stand out by contrast.

::: {.business-case}
**Brand candour and leader communication.** Brands sometimes admit a minor weakness
to make their strengths more credible. Avis's long-running campaign built around
being "No. 2" in car rentals, created by the agency Doyle Dane Bernbach in the 1960s,
is a widely cited example of turning an admitted limitation into a reason to believe
the brand's promise to "try harder". In product reviews, research on blemishing
suggests that a mostly positive review profile with a few mild criticisms can be
more persuasive than uniformly glowing reviews. For leaders, the pratfall effect
suggests that acknowledging a minor error can increase warmth, but only when
competence is already established and the error does not touch the core of the role.
A chief financial officer who misspeaks a statistic in a speech may seem human. One
who misstates earnings does not.
:::

## Using Named Effects Responsibly {#effects-replication}

Named effects are attractive because they are memorable, specific, and easy to
apply. The same features make them easy to misuse. Three cautions follow from the
evidence reviewed in this chapter.

First, **effects vary in robustness**. Anchoring replicated robustly across many
laboratories [@klein2014], and mere exposure rests on a large meta-analytic base
[@bornstein1989; @montoya2017]. By contrast, the attraction effect is sensitive to
how options are presented [@frederick2014], the glass cliff depends on context
[@morgenroth2020], and the pratfall effect depends on the observer
[@helmreich1970]. The catalogue at the start of this chapter rates evidence strength
for this reason. See the discussion of the [replication crisis](#replication-crisis)
for general principles.

Second, **effects need mechanisms**. An effect tells us *that* something happens. A
mechanism tells us *when* it will happen. The mere exposure effect is useful to a
media planner only together with the two-factor account that predicts wear-out. The
decoy effect is useful to a pricing manager only with the boundary conditions that
determine whether customers will notice dominance. Linking each effect to a theory
, fluency, prospect theory, signaling, social identity, is what turns a list of
curiosities into a toolkit.

Third, **effects interact and sometimes conflict**. Familiarity breeds liking (mere
exposure), but too much familiarity breeds boredom (Goldilocks, Coolidge). Typical
designs are attractive (beauty in averageness), but distinctiveness signals status
(snob effect). The resolution is rarely to choose one effect over another. It is to
specify the conditions, the stage of exposure, the consumer segment, the
observability of consumption, under which each dominates.

## Chapter Summary {#effects-summary}

::: {.key-takeaways}
- A **named effect** is an empirical regularity. Its value depends on the mechanism
  that explains it and the boundary conditions that limit it.
- **Mere exposure** increases liking, but repetition eventually produces tedium. The
  two-factor curve underlies wear-in and wear-out in advertising
  [@zajonc1968; @bornstein1989; @cacioppo1979].
- The **warm-glow heuristic** runs the other way, liking increases perceived
  familiarity [@Monin_2003], and must not be confused with Andreoni's warm-glow
  giving [@andreoni1990].
- **Goldilocks** (inverted-U) patterns describe preference for moderate novelty and
  complexity [@berlyne1970; @McCall_1977; @kidd2012], while **beauty in averageness**
  shows that typical stimuli are attractive [@langlois1990]. The two are reconciled by
  treating typicality and novelty as separate dimensions [@hekkert2003].
- **Bandwagon, snob, and Veblen effects** make demand depend on others' consumption
  and on price itself [@Leibenstein_1950], with opposite implications for scarcity and
  mass-market strategies.
- The **glass cliff** describes the disproportionate appointment of women and
  minorities to precarious leadership roles [@Ryan_2005; @Ryan_2016; @cook2014].
- The **IKEA effect**, **decoy effect**, **anchoring**, and **pratfall effect** offer
  practical levers for product design, pricing, negotiation, and communication: each
  with documented limits [@norton2012; @huber1982; @frederick2014; @tversky1974;
  @aronson1966].
:::

## Discussion Questions {#effects-questions}

1. The mere exposure effect and the Goldilocks effect make apparently opposite
   predictions about the effect of familiarity. Specify the conditions under which
   each should dominate, and design an advertising experiment to test them.
2. A brand-tracking survey shows that a brand's familiarity and favourability have
   both risen. Using the warm-glow heuristic and mere exposure, explain why the causal
   direction is ambiguous. How would you design a study to separate the two?
3. A luxury fashion brand is considering launching a lower-priced line. Use
   Leibenstein's framework to predict the effects on existing and new customers. What
   evidence would tell you whether the snob or the Veblen effect is more important for
   this brand?
4. Archival and experimental studies of the glass cliff do not always agree. What are
   the strengths and weaknesses of each design, and what data would provide the most
   convincing test?
5. Following the 2014 debate about the attraction effect, what conditions would you
   check before recommending a decoy pricing tier to a client? How would you test the
   recommendation in the field?
6. Choose two effects from this chapter that could be explained by processing
   fluency. Explain how fluency accounts for each, and identify one finding that a
   fluency account cannot easily explain.

## Further Reading {#effects-reading}

- @zajonc1968: the original monograph on mere exposure, combining correlational and
  experimental evidence.
- @bornstein1989: the classic meta-analysis that identifies the moderators of the
  exposure effect.
- @Leibenstein_1950: a short, clear treatment of bandwagon, snob, and Veblen effects
  that remains the starting point for social effects in demand.
- @Ryan_2016: a review of a decade of glass cliff research, its explanations, and its
  impact.
- @norton2012: the experiments that named the IKEA effect and identified completion as
  a boundary condition.
- @frederick2014: a careful challenge to the robustness of the attraction effect, best
  read together with @huber2014.
- @ariely2003: an elegant demonstration that preferences can be coherent yet
  arbitrary.
- @langlois1990: the composite-face studies that launched research on beauty in
  averageness.
